opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, one of the earliest signals was just how much we were using it ourselves. Before we launched, people on the team, and then more broadly around the company, kept coming back to it for real tasks, not just to test it. When people start reaching for an internal prototype because it actually saves them time, that's a pretty good sign.

Then, once we got it into more people's hands, what struck me was how varied the use cases were. We'd built it with knowledge work in mind: market research, literature reviews, that kind of thing. But people were using it for very personal things too. Researching a medical diagnosis for a family member, comparing products before a big purchase, planning a trip, digging into some niche hobby. People would tell us it found things they wouldn't have found on their own, or that it did in ten minutes what would have taken them hours or days.

The other signal was how people talked about the outputs. They weren't saying "this is a neat demo." They were saying "I sent this report to my team," or "I used this to make a decision." When people are willing to act on what it produces, and they trust it enough because it cites its sources and they can check them, that's when you know it's genuinely useful and not just impressive.

r001.rationale: The candidate cites internal adoption, diverse use cases, time savings, and people acting on sourced reports as signals of usefulness. It does not mention users asking for access to be restored during outages.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the earliest sign came before we shipped anything externally. While we were building it, people on the team kept using the prototype for their own stuff. Not for demos, not to test it, but because they actually wanted the answer. Someone would be researching which apartment to rent, or trying to understand some obscure part of the tax code, or comparing a bunch of medical studies for a family member, and they'd just reach for it instead of opening twenty browser tabs. When a tool you're building becomes something your own colleagues quietly depend on, that's usually a pretty good signal.

The other thing that stood out was how people reacted to waiting. We were nervous about that. The model goes off for five, ten, sometimes twenty minutes, and we assumed users would hate it. But once people got a result that was genuinely thorough, something with real citations they could click through and verify, they stopped minding. They'd kick off a query and go do something else. It felt more like delegating a task than using a search box, and the fact that people adapted their behavior to that so quickly told us the value was there.

And then after launch, we started seeing a lot of use cases we hadn't anticipated. People doing due diligence on companies, academics catching up on a literature, folks shopping for very specific products with weird constraints. The common thread was that these were all things where you'd normally spend hours, and the cost of getting it wrong was high enough that people cared about sourcing. That's exactly the kind of problem it was designed for, so seeing it show up organically was really encouraging.

r001.rationale: The response cites teammates using the prototype, adapting to long waits, and post-launch use cases as signals of usefulness. It does not mention users asking for access to be restored during outages.
